title: Doubling, the Uncanny and the Creature's Voice
welcome_lead: Examine the Gothic motif of the doppelganger in Frankenstein and analyse how the Creature's eloquence subverts his monstrosity.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on doubling, the uncanny, and the Creature's eloquence in Shelley's Frankenstein.
final_note: The Creature speaks Miltonic English in the Alps; Victor mostly screams. Shelley invites us to ask who, in fact, is the monster.

concepts.def: Gothic figure of the double or shadow self; Victor and the Creature are read as halves of a single divided psyche.

walkthroughs.body_html: Critics from Masao Miyoshi to Anne K. Mellor read Victor and the Creature as psychological doubles. The Creature appears at moments of Victor's deepest crisis (after Justine's execution; on the wedding night). He is Victor's repressed: the body Victor denies, the responsibility Victor refuses. The novel's Gothic logic insists that what is disowned returns, embodied, demanding recognition.

The Creature's narrative (Chapters 11–16) is delivered in articulate, often Miltonic English. He references Paradise Lost, Goethe's Werther, and Plutarch's Lives — texts found in a portmanteau in the woods. His eloquence subverts the visual horror Victor projects on him. Critics including Peter Brooks argue the Creature's mastery of language is precisely what makes his exclusion intolerable: he claims humanity through speech.

In Chapter 20, on a remote Orkney island, Victor begins assembling a female companion at the Creature's request, then destroys her, fearing 'a race of devils'. The destruction provokes the Creature's vow — 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night' — and Elizabeth's eventual murder. Mellor reads Victor's refusal as a horror of female reproductive autonomy: he cannot bear creating a being he cannot control.

mcqs.q: What are conventions of the Gothic genre?
options: The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
Gothic just means scary stories with vampires and ghosts.
Settings of ruin and decay, supernatural or psychological terror, transgression of boundaries, the sublime, doubled or haunted protagonists, and atmospheric excess.
Gothic refers to medieval architecture, not literature.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.

mcqs.q: Why distinguish the speaker of a poem from the poet?
options: The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The speaker is the voice constructed in the poem; the poet is the writer. Treating them as identical can mislead, especially with dramatic monologues or personae.
The speaker of a poem is always the poet themselves.
